newsitem.title: CONGO: Sleepy Sunday in Brazzaville's stalemated civil war.
newsitem.headline: Sleepy Sunday in Brazzaville's stalemated civil war.

text.p: Congo's warring rivals let their weapons rest on Sunday but real peace seemed as far away as ever despite the latest ceasefire.
Though rare bursts of gunfire persisted, the capital Brazzaville had one of its calmest days in a bloody civil war throughout June, after a new truce agreed late on Friday.
The city has been devastated and many hundreds of its residents killed in the conflict in which neither side has a clear upper hand.
Both President Pascal Lissouba and his adversary, former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso, say they want the same thing -- free and fair presidential elections.
But Lissouba claims Sassou has staged a coup attempt, while Sassou says Lissouba provoked the crisis as a pretext for extending his term in office that was to have ended next month.
"Things have not advanced much," said one French official. "The positions of both sides are still very far apart."
France, the former colonial power, has kept its embassy open in Brazzaville even though all other missions fled.
Its ambassador Raymond Cesaire is effectively blocked in the building in the disputed heart of the city.
Lissouba troops stopped him leaving for the relative safety of his residence, a wartime home of "Free French" leader General Charles de Gaulle, on Saturday.
Pope John Paul appealed to the warring factions in the city to stop fighting and take up the challenge of a peaceful solution.

Speaking to pilgrims and tourists in St Peter's Square in the Vatican for his Sunday blessing, the 77-year-old Pontiff expressed concern that the conflict was blocking mediation efforts and the work of humanitarian organisations.

"I add my voice to the appeals by the bishops of Congo so that so many brothers and sisters may be spared suffering and so much mourning and that a peaceful solution to the crisis can be found soon," he said.
Rival military chiefs agreed on Friday to a new week-long truce after earlier ones collapsed.
It came after a deafening but inconclusive artillery battle for the airport, held by Lissouba, on Wednesday and Thursday.
That battle sent tens of thousands of civilians fleeing the city after once safe outer suburbs came under shelling.

The rival chiefs-of-staff also backed a mediators' plan that called for peace, demilitarisation of the airport to allow a planned U.N.-led peacekeeping force to be deployed, and a unity government to get the elections back on track.
"The national mediation committee is elated that the parties in conflict have accepted its nine-point plan," said a spokesman for neutral mayor, Bernard Kolelas.
Togo and Senegal say they would join a U.N. force but none will be send until the fighting subsides.
The charismatic Sassou ruled a Marxist one-party state for 13 years until yielding to free elections in 1992 that Lissouba, a former plant geneticist, won.
The parties that sprung up with democracy have won support on largely ethnic lines.
